title: Atlas and Harbor
premise: In 1918, in a fog-bound harbor city where the Meridian Trading Company owns everything from the cranes to the constables, Bram Voss — raised by pearl divers, indentured at nine, and now the company's most trusted courier of sealed orders — is handed a ledger page bearing the handwriting of Aldous Wren, the company clerk who drowned six months ago. The stranger who brings it, a one-armed cartographer named Ilsa Rehn, claims Wren is alive and hiding evidence that the company has been selling armistice intelligence to both sides. As Bram and Ilsa race to finish copying Wren's hidden records before the armistice signing — and before the company burns its own workshop to erase them — Bram must choose between the only family he's ever had inside the company walls and a ragtag found family of divers, forgers, and dockworkers who believe justice can exist outside the law. The book ends with the workshop burning on schedule but the copies already at sea; the company's directors fall to a public inquiry, Bram walks free with his indenture voided, and he stands on the breakwater at dawn, finally measuring the world in what cannot be taken.
about_author: K. M. Yarrow is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing shipping ledgers from the Great War era. They write historical fiction about the people history files under 'miscellaneous labor.'

chapters.title: The Weight of Sealed Things
chapters.summary: Bram Voss's POV. We meet him running sealed orders through the fog-bound port, trusted precisely because he is owned — indentured, expendable, invisible. He measures his life in what can be carried: a knife, a mother's pearl, a ledger habit. When he's summoned to deliver orders he isn't allowed to read, he notices the seal is wrong. Emotional beat: quiet unease beneath practiced obedience.

chapters.title: A Stranger with Dead Man's Ink
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A one-armed woman, Ilsa Rehn, corners him at the diver's jetty with a letter in the unmistakable hand of Aldous Wren — the clerk whose funeral Bram attended. She asks him to verify the handwriting against company archives, a crime for an indentured man. He refuses, then finds the same handwriting on the orders he delivered. Emotional beat: the ground tilting; loyalty beginning to crack.

chapters.title: What the Company Owns
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. Her backstory surfaces: she mapped coastlines for the company until Wren showed her what the ledgers hid — armistice intelligence sold to both belligerents. Now she needs someone inside the counting-house. She watches Bram navigate the company's web of debts and favors and understands his cage better than he does. Emotional beat: wary recognition between two people shaped by the same machine.

chapters.title: The Diver's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. He visits his mother's old diving crew, now blacklisted by the company, and learns how Wren survived the staged drowning — pulled half-dead from the bay by divers the company had ruined. The divers hide Wren below the breakwater. For the first time, Bram sees a family held together by choice rather than contract. Emotional beat: longing for belonging outside ownership.

chapters.title: Orders Come Down
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The company hands Bram his gravest commission: escort the burn crew to the harbor workshop where Wren's original records are stored, to be destroyed before the armistice delegation arrives. He accepts — and secretly signals Ilsa. His handler, the affable Director Corvane, praises him in a way that feels like being petted. Emotional beat: complicity and dread braided together.

chapters.title: Copying by Candlelight
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. In the flooded cellar beneath the workshop, Ilsa, Bram, and the divers begin copying Wren's ledgers by night — a race against ink, damp, and the armistice clock. A near-discovery by a night watchman forces them to improvise, and Bram's knowledge of the building's rhythms saves them. Emotional beat: found family forged in shared risk; trust becoming love without either naming it.

chapters.title: The Handler's Kindness
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. Corvane reveals he has always known about Bram's mother, her debts, her death — kindness as leash. He offers Bram freedom papers if he names the corpse-peddlers spreading Wren's 'forgeries.' Bram realizes his entire life has been managed as an investment. He lies smoothly for the first time and hates how good it feels. Emotional beat: corruption glimpsed from the inside.

chapters.title: Betrayal at Low Tide
chapters.summary: Ilsa's POV. One of the diving crew, desperate to redeem his blacklist status, sells the location of the cellar. The company raids it; Wren is captured alive, and Ilsa barely escapes with half-finished copies. Bram learns his forged delivery route was used to trace them — his own competence weaponized. Emotional beat: devastation, guilt, and the hard choice between flight and rescue.

chapters.title: The Workshop Burns
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, climax. On the eve of the armistice signing, the company torches the workshop with Wren locked inside. Bram goes back for him through the smoke, using every secret passage he was trained to know, while Ilsa holds the last copy pages above the tideline. They pull Wren out as the roof falls; the burning ledgers light the harbor like a false dawn. Emotional beat: fury transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: What Cannot Be Carried
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, resolution. The copied ledgers reach the armistice delegation by fishing boat; the inquiry breaks the company, voids the indentures, and frees Bram along with every diver and dockworker it owned. Corvane faces the courts he once bought. On the breakwater at dawn, Bram gives his mother's pearl to the sea and keeps instead the things that can't be carried: names, debts repaid, a family chosen. Emotional beat: grief settled into peace.
